a shared escaping helper used by two units
pitfalls: unescape order: "~01" must give "~1" (left-to-right single pass, not replace ~1 then ~0 naively on a mutated buffer)
a "~" that is last or followed by anything but 0/1 (including "/") is invalid
"" is valid and parses to an empty list; "/" is one empty token; "//" two
a non-empty pointer without a leading "/" is an Err
ptr_append escapes only the new token, never p; ptr_append validates p but not the token
ptr_parent of "/a" is "", of "" is Err, of an invalid pointer is Err
list.push prepends, so tokens must be pushed in reverse
freeing: every token box, every list cell, and the buffers are owned
indexing past the end on a trailing "~" (must not panic)
the nested Box shape for tokens (#461)
difficulty_notes: Logic is easy (a scan and two escapes); the difficulty is cancho's ownership shapes: a list of owned byte runs (Box[Box[[byte]]]) and Buffer threading, and a Result carrying a borrowed sub-slice. Six units: valid and push_token are helpers (ptr_valid, ptr_push_token) that the plan names so parse, format and append share one definition of validity and of escaping; the audit grades only the four brief functions (oracle.py vendored unchanged, 134 cases) plus a 26-case round-trip group (the brief's two properties on the oracle's own inputs), 160 in all. The plan samples about 25 tests across the units and overlaps the brief's own worked examples; hidden cases are the other ~120 (every GOOD x 5 tokens for append, the invalid-pointer variants, non-ASCII, ~ edge cases).
